correctness.rationale: Oddness of n^2+n-1 forces tau(n) odd, hence n square. Any prime r dividing tau(n) must therefore see a nonzero quadratic-residue root of x^2+x-1. For primes below 19 only r=11 can do so. Consequently tau(n)<209 forces tau(n)=11 or 121; the complete divisor-count shapes for those values all give n congruent to 1 modulo 11, contradicting divisibility. The family p^10*31^18 has tau=209 and is divisible modulo both 11 and 19 exactly as claimed.

value.rationale: The source paper explicitly highlights x^2+x-1 as having no nontrivial example through 10^8 and asks for possible divisor-count values. The exact minimum 209 gives the first nontrivial point of that spectrum, proves infinitely many examples exist far beyond the searched range, and explains the computational gap. This is a natural exact invariant tied directly to an explicit open problem rather than an arbitrary finite slice.
